newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S.-Russian space crew face new problem on Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Russian space crew face new problem on Mir.

text.p: The crippled Mir space station was hit by a new navigational problem on Thursday but mission control said the Russian-American crew were in no danger and continued to practise for repair work next week.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told Reuters there was an unexplained malfunction in all the station's gyrodines -- devices that keep Mir's solar panels lined up to the Sun to gain maximum power as the station hurtles round the Earth.
The result was that the cosmonauts were having to fire their rocket engines to keep Mir lined up to the Sun and prevent a further loss of electric power.
The station lost up to half its power last week after a collision with an unmanned cargo craft punctured one its modules and cut of supplies from some panels.

"Mir is on its set orbit, but we're having to fire the engines more often. All the gyrodines are malfunctioning," Krikalyov said. Mission Control near Moscow, rather than the three-man crew on Mir, was dealing with the problem.
"It presents no danger either for the station or the cosmonauts as we have enough fuel," Krikalyov said. "But it is unpleasant."
Krikalyov said the reason for the gyrodine malfunction was not known.

The ageing station has been in a vicious circle in which the loss of electric power has made it harder to power the gyrodines and keep the station in line with the Sun. That in turn had further reduced power.
Mir can use its rocket engines to adjust its alignment, but fuel supplies are always limited.
A cargo craft is due to blast off form Earth on Saturday carrying supplies to repair the damaged electric power system. It should take two days to reach Mir.

The voices of the crew -- commander Vasily Tsibliyev, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin and British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale -- sounded calm during conversations on Thursday with Mission Control which were monitored by journalists.

Much of their time is now taken up with preparing for repair work next week, when the two Russians will have to enter the now sealed-off and air-free Spektr module in bulky spacesuits and attempt to reconnect its solar panels with the main batteries.
"Get down to the controls, and after lunch you will continue with the spacesuits," one ground operator told the crew.
Krikalyov said working with the spacesuits -- which will require special modifying devices being brought up on the supply craft -- was now the cosmonauts' main activity.
There will be very little room to work in the module wearing the suits but Krikalyov and a fellow cosmonaut on the ground had made trials on a mock-up of the station and proved it could be done.
"We simulated the situation the cosmonauts are going to experience and we drew the conclusion that, in practice, they can enter the module with their spacesuits on," he said.
